title: Sparse Transfer Hypothesis for WLT‑Nets
content: Assumption 1 (the "sparse transfer hypothesis") states the following concrete condition for treating a pruned subnetwork as a transferable winning lottery ticket (WLT‑net). Let D denote a domain represented by D = {χ, P(X)} where χ is the input space and P(X) is the input distribution, and let a task T be represented by T = {y, f(x)} where y is the label space and f(x) is the network mapping from inputs x∈χ to labels. Let T_S be a dense source network with parameters {λ_i} trained on a source domain D_S and let T_T be a candidate sparse target network represented as ξ(x; M(λ_i)) obtained by applying an unstructured mask M(λ_i)=m ⊙ λ_i with m ∈ {0,1}^{|λ|}. Denote by n_S and n_T the numbers of training iterations required for T_S and T_T, respectively, to reach their minimum validation loss, and denote by η_S and η_T the corresponding validation accuracy percentages. If (i) ξ(x; M(λ_i)) can be obtained from T_S by unstructured pruning using a mask m ∈ {0,1}^{|λ|}, (ii) after retraining the pruned network the minimum‑validation loss is reached in no more iterations than the dense source (n_T ≤ n_S), and (iii) after retraining the pruned network the validation accuracy is no worse than the dense source (η_T ≥ η_S), then ξ(x; M(λ_i)) is regarded as a WLT‑net of T_S that retains the source task's representational capacity and therefore can serve as a sparse object for transfer learning from D_S to D_T.

title: WLTs‑SDTL Algorithm with Optimized Pruning and Parameter Handling
content:
The WLTs‑SDTL algorithm for sparse deep transfer learning iteratively produces a transferable sparse subnetwork and transfers it to a target task as follows. During source training, denote by λ_i the initial weight of a parameter, by λ_n the parameter value at the iteration when validation loss is minimized (after n iterations), and by λ_α an intermediate parameter value recorded at some earlier iteration index α with α < n for late reset. Define the per‑weight rating score
      μ(λ_i) = max(0, (λ_i λ_n) / |λ_i|),
      which evaluates each parameter by combining its initial sign with its value at the end of training (so μ(λ_i) equals max(0, sign(λ_i)·λ_n)). At each pruning round, compute μ for all parameters, set a layerwise pruning rate p (percentage of weights to retain per layer), and form a binary mask m ∈ {0,1}^{|λ|} by keeping the top p% weights per layer according to μ (m = 1 for retained weights, m = 0 for pruned weights). After pruning, reset unpruned parameters (those with m = 1) to the recorded intermediate weights λ_α (late reset with α < n) before the next training phase to accelerate convergence and improve final accuracy. For pruned parameters (m = 0), evaluate the parameter's observed training variation trend: if the parameter's observed values during training tended toward zero, freeze that parameter at zero for all subsequent training; otherwise freeze that parameter at its initial value λ_i. Repeat ranking, pruning, reset, and freezing until the desired sparse subnetwork ξ is obtained. Transfer the final sparse subnetwork ξ to the target domain D_T as the target model T_T and fine‑tune it on D_T while keeping convolutional layers frozen and updating only the unfrozen parameters (for example, the final fully connected layer) according to the experimental protocol.

title: Sparse Subnetwork Performance on CIFAR‑10 Benchmark
content: Using CIFAR‑10 as the source domain D_S and a ResNet‑18 backbone (the 18‑layer residual network with approximately 11,173,962 total parameters in the original dense configuration), iterative unstructured pruning with the WLTs‑SDTL procedure produced a WLT‑net that retained 10.7% of the original parameters (1,212,145 parameters retained out of 11,173,962). This pruned ResNet‑18 WLT‑net achieved an average test accuracy of 89.24% on CIFAR‑10, which compares to the original dense ResNet‑18's average test accuracy of 89.43% on the same dataset and evaluation metric.

title: Transferability of Sparse WLT‑Nets on SmallNORB
content: When the sparse WLT‑net obtained by pruning a CIFAR‑10 ResNet‑18 source was transferred to SmallNORB as the target domain D_T and fine‑tuned according to the WLTs‑SDTL protocol (transfer initialization from recorded λ_α, frozen convolutional layers, and tuning only the unfrozen layers such as the final fully connected layer), the WLTs‑SDTL method that includes late reset and weight‑trend‑aware freezing produced target accuracies that are comparable to or exceed the accuracy achieved by training a dense ResNet‑18 from scratch on SmallNORB (the dense from‑scratch baseline achieved 89.9% average accuracy in the reported experiments), while using substantially fewer trainable parameters in the transferred sparse network.

title: Plant Disease Identification with Sparse DTL on Tomato Leaves
content: Applied to tomato leaf disease classification using a filtered and balanced subset of the PlantVillage dataset (images resized to 64×64 and per‑class training sets adjusted to 1,500 images for the selected classes), WLTs‑SDTL produced sparse ResNet‑18 models whose peak reported performance occurred when 67% of the original parameters were removed (i.e., 33% of parameters retained), giving a peak test accuracy of 97.69%. At an extreme sparsity level produced by 15 rounds of iterative pruning, when only 3.6% of the original ResNet‑18 parameters remained (406,495 retained parameters out of 11,173,962), the sparse model still attained 93.16% test accuracy on the same evaluation, demonstrating that a highly compressed network produced by WLTs‑SDTL can sustain acceptable classification performance for this agricultural task.

title: Sparse Transfer for Citrus Greening Detection with Optimal Pruning Range
content: For citrus greening (Huanglongbing) detection using a combined training set formed from 1,500 field‑clipped images derived from 1,266 collected field images and 5,000 randomly sampled PlantVillage orange leaf images (6,500 training samples total), transferring a sparse WLT‑net initialized from a pretrained related task on PlantVillage produced the following results in the reported experiments: a peak accuracy of 98.26% was obtained at the 3rd pruning level when 51.2% of the original ResNet‑18 parameters remained; this 98.26% peak exceeds the dense DTL baseline accuracy of 98.06% obtained when the dense ResNet‑18 was initialized from the more similar pretrained task. The experiments show that fine‑grained pruning in the approximate retained‑parameter range 50%–30% consistently produced optimal or near‑optimal performance for this task. Even at extreme compression levels, a model retaining 8.59% of parameters achieved 96.67% accuracy and a model retaining 3.6% of parameters achieved 94.01% accuracy on the same evaluation; both of these sparse models obtained higher accuracy than a dense ResNet‑18 trained from scratch without transfer in the reported experiments.
